title: Trump, Elections and Democracy: How We Can Move Beyond Electoral Fetishism
author: Richard Rubenstein
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/01/IMG_4541-680x510.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/29/trump-
elections-and-democracy-how-we-can-move-beyond-electoral-fetishism/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/01/IMG_4541-680x510.jpg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

Donald Trump’s much ballyhooed public address on July 16 – an attempt to
pressure Congress to approve his “Save America” election legislation – turned
out to be a pitiful bust. Even Sean Hannity seemed embarrassed by a speech
that claimed large‑scale “election vulnerabilities,” including hundreds of
thousands of alleged non‑citizen votes and Chinese hacking of voter files but
offered zero evidence of fraud in the 2020 presidential election.

Evidence or no evidence, Trump can’t stop alleging that the vote for Biden was
rigged – a compulsive accusation that anti-Trumpers attribute to his inability
to accept defeat, his delusional tendencies, and his intention to challenge
the results of the upcoming federal midterm elections. The president’s bad
motives and psychological _mischigas_ are undeniable. Even so, his election
denialism has significant causes that most Democrats avoid mentioning, since
to do so could expose their own role in provoking the madness of King Donald.

Where the election of 2020 is concerned, the president is quite crazed – but
what drove him around the bend? Most critics seem determined to forget that
the original trauma in this case – the first serious allegations of a rigged
election casting doubt on the authenticity of the voting process – were the
charges made by Democratic leaders and pursued by various “deep state”
agencies under Joe Biden that Trump and his campaign had conspired with the
Russians to defeat Hilary Clinton in 2016.

How could a vulgar upstart and political amateur like Trump defeat a seasoned
professional like Hilary? It must have been a Russian plot! Few Democrats
these days have much to say about “Russiagate.” They seem to have difficulty
remembering that during the 2016 campaign the DNC hired a former British spy
to compile evidence of a Trump-Russia conspiracy (the “Steele Dossier”) while
encouraging F.B.I. director James Comey to begin a major investigation of his
own. The Steele dossier turned out to be weakly sourced and unreliable. After
the election Democratic-controlled congressional committees held extensive
hearings on the matter, also without significant results. And after two years
more of further investigation, Special Counsel Robert Mueller issued a report
stating that Russian agencies had indeed attempted to interfere with the
election, but that evidence of a conspiracy implicating the Trump campaign was
lacking.

All that work to “explain” Trump’s election – and with such disappointing
results! Not only was the conspiracy unproved, but there was no evidence at
all that Russian interference had had a measurable impact on the 2016
election. In that year six key industrial states that had voted for Obama four
years earlier went for Trump by substantial majorities – not because of
Russian trolls or hacked Clinton emails, but because so many working people
felt that the Democrats had abandoned them. Even so, the losers could not
resist charging, in effect, that the election had been “rigged” by Trump and
the Russians.

It seems clear, in retrospect, that the Russiagate allegations were hardly
more substantial than Trump’s subsequent insistence that the election of 2020
had been stolen. But today’s Democratic leaders take no responsibility for
attempting to delegitimize a winning presidential candidate by casting doubt
on the validity of the electoral process. Nor, even if “progressives,” will
they admit that any of the criminal charges brought against Trump in the Biden
era were hostile exercises of prosecutorial discretion. Anti-Trumpers tend to
attribute their nemesis’s obsessiveness and vengefulness exclusively to his
own defects of character. These defects, God knows, are plentiful. But it's
U.S. political institutions, not just Donald J. Trump’s personality, that are
deformed. And most of his adversaries don’t seem to want to deal with _that_
reality at all.

When Trump says that elections are rigged and proposes “reforms” that would
suppress voter participation, one’s impulse is to spring to the defense of the
current electoral system. There is certainly reason to suspect that the
president is an authoritarian operator who would happily rig an election
himself rather than surrender power. His fake reforms should be strongly
opposed, of course. But electoral fetishism is not an effective response to
his election denialism. The system as it stands _is_ rigged in favor of
candidates and policies favored by the capitalist elite: the oligarchs and
their political servitors. It _does_ need to be changed, although surely not
in the ways Trump is proposing. Three sources of electoral corruption deserve
particular notice: _U.S._ constitutional and legal norms, an evenly divided
electorate, and Big Money.

> 1) The U.S. Constitution is a document that was intended to consolidate the
> gains of the American Revolution while preventing power from falling into
> the hands of the “mob.” As a result, even after enfranchising women, former
> slaves, and poor people, we have inherited a presidential electoral system
> that makes it possible to win an election by millions of popular votes but
> still lose the presidency. Our senatorial voting system gives equal
> representation to Wyoming’s half million residents and 34.5 million
> Californians, while the rules of apportionment approved by the U.S. Supreme
> Court permit the outrageously partisan (and racist) gerrymandering of
> legislative electoral districts by those in power. Meanwhile, a “winner-
> take-all” norm in almost all U.S. elections assures that groups constituting
> a voting minority will be subject for years to the dictates of those
> constituting a majority – even if the election was decided by a few hundred
> or a few thousand votes bought or coerced by powerful interests.
>
> 2) In fact, when the electorate is evenly divided, a little fraud can go a
> long way. Donald Trump’s partisans are unable to prove that illegal voting
> played a significant role in any recent election – but the idea that a
> relative handful of illicit votes can swing a closely fought contest is far
> from a paranoid fantasy. As Tracy Campbell shows in her richly documented
> study, _Deliver the Vote_(2005), serious electoral fraud has been “an
> American tradition” since colonial times. One recalls the presidential
> election of 1960, when John Kennedy defeated Richard Nixon in Illinois by
> 8,858 votes out of almost 5 million cast. That result was confirmed only
> after Chicago’s mayor Richard J. Daley, who had delayed reporting the city’s
> vote until the downstate (mainly Republican) vote had been calculated,
> announced it. Some Republicans charged fraud both in Illinois and in Texas,
> where the Democratic machine was also very powerful, but post-election
> investigations were half-hearted, no “smoking gun” proving significant
> wrongdoing was discovered, and Nixon – unlike Trump – was not inclined to
> pursue the matter after his rival was inaugurated.
>
> 3) More important than this potential for electoral fraud, however, is the
> permeation of American elections by Big Money: a form of legalized
> corruption that gives the oligarchic elite and its political representatives
> decisive influence over the ideas and behavior of U.S. political parties,
> candidates for office, and voters. Private campaign contributions have
> always been an outsized influence on U.S. elections, but In _Citizens
> United_ and subsequent legal cases, the U.S. Supreme Court confirmed the
> rights of wealthy individuals and corporations to engage in a range of
> practices that includes creating super-PACS and funneling “dark money” into
> political campaigns. The floodgates opened, and in 2024 Elon Musk alone
> contributed around $290 million in various forms to the campaigns of Trump
> and other Republican candidates.

In the same election the Harris campaign outspent that of Trump by almost half
a billion dollars . . . and still lost. The moral: U.S. elections are
corrupted not so much by simple vote-buying as by a system that permits an
elite to establish the political and ideological ground rules which limit the
choices of “acceptable” candidates and policies available to voters. A major
purpose of these rules is to keep the oligarchs’ basic “rights” to own and
control great accumulations of capital from being subjected to challenge by
elected officials.

The current turmoil in the United States, with President Trump’s popularity
declining and many Democrats moving somewhat to the left, provides an
interesting test of how the system works. Even though the Democratic Party’s
self-declared “democratic socialists” are little more than outspoken liberals,
Trump and the Heritage Foundation have started to call them communists. So
far, this name-calling has not been accompanied by much repression, probably
because most oligarchs understand that Bernie Sanders or AOC-style
progressivism does not seriously threaten their ownership or management
privileges. If these privileges are brought into question, however, a
different line is likely to be drawn, and repressive measures initiated.

Many Democrats and some Republicans want to increase taxes on the rich,
provide a wider range of public welfare services to working people, regulate
big corporations more effectively, and shift resources from military to
peacetime uses. Since the New Deal, the corporate elite has considered such
demands negotiable rather than taboo. But if political organizers wish to go
further, say, by capping or confiscating great wealth, advocating the public
ownership of key resources, greatly reducing military-industrial expenditures,
or redefining management rights (including the “right” to buy political
candidates), the situation is likely to change. An oligarchy feeling genuinely
threatened will define such activists as unAmerican extremists and subject
them to McCarthy-style repression, or worse.

Is a mass-based anti-capitalist mobilization possible? I think so. Especially
if the world capitalist system has entered a period of crisis that some
theorists believe can only get worse, moderate reforms of the sort favored by
Democratic progressives are likely to prove ineffective, and organizers
proposing more radical changes could find themselves leading a mass movement.
The fear that a genuine Left could emerge in the U.S. motivates fascistic
representatives of the oligarchy like Stephen Miller to propose preemptive
repression -- including measures intended to “fix” the electoral rules. But
the answer to such threats is not just to condemn Miller, and certainly not to
sacralize the pre-Trump voting system.

For now, elements of the old system such as mail-in ballots must be protected
against Trumpian vote-suppressing tactics. But the point of doing this is to
lay the groundwork for a transformation that will break the power of the
oligarchy and turn elections into a genuine method (among others) of self-
rule. Our guiding aim cannot be simply to “defend” a deeply compromised
democracy. It must be to create a real one.
